items.stem: In the summer of 1955, a few months before her arrest in Montgomery, Rosa Parks attended a two-week workshop on desegregation at an institution in Tennessee that trained organisers in the struggle to secure civil rights for African Americans. Which one?
items.stemEs: En el verano de 1955, pocos meses antes de su detención en Montgomery, Rosa Parks asistió a un taller de dos semanas sobre la eliminación de la segregación en una institución de Tennessee que formaba organizadores en la lucha por los derechos civiles de los afroamericanos. ¿Cuál era?

choices.text: Fisk University in Nashville, whose students were trained in nonviolent protest and led the city's sit-ins
choices.textEs: La Universidad Fisk de Nashville, cuyos estudiantes fueron formados en la protesta no violenta y dirigieron las sentadas de la ciudad
choices.explanation: Both halves are true and Fisk students were central to the Nashville sit-ins of 1960. Those students were trained in church basement workshops run by James Lawson, and the 1955 workshop in the question was somewhere else.
choices.misconception: names the Tennessee campus most associated with the movement for a workshop held elsewhere in the state

choices.text: The Highlander Folk School at Monteagle
choices.textEs: La Escuela Popular Highlander de Monteagle

choices.text: Tennessee Agricultural and Industrial State University, which sent students into the Nashville sit-ins and the Freedom Rides
choices.textEs: La Universidad Estatal Agrícola e Industrial de Tennessee, que envió estudiantes a las sentadas de Nashville y a los Viajes de la Libertad
choices.explanation: True — students from the school now called Tennessee State were expelled for taking part and several went on to the Freedom Rides. It is a university that supplied participants, not the residential school that ran the 1955 workshop.
choices.misconception: answers with an institution whose students joined the movement rather than the one that trained its organisers

choices.text: Tuskegee Institute, in the Alabama town where Rosa Parks was born
choices.textEs: El Instituto Tuskegee, en el pueblo de Alabama donde nació Rosa Parks
choices.explanation: Tuskegee is real, Parks was born there, and the connection is genuine. It is in Alabama, and the question asks for the institution in Tennessee.
choices.misconception: follows the personal connection to the wrong state

items.dokRationale: Recall of one institution by name and role. The student matches a person to a place; no reasoning about how economic or legal pressure worked is involved. A DOK 2 item on this standard requires that reasoning.
items.explanation: The school at Monteagle had been running workshops since 1932, and from 1953 it turned them toward desegregation — which is why a great many of the people who led the next decade had been through the same rooms. Tennessee revoked its charter and seized the property in 1961; it reopened near Knoxville and continues today at New Market.
items.explanationEs: La escuela de Monteagle venía dando talleres desde 1932, y a partir de 1953 los orientó hacia la eliminación de la segregación; por eso muchísimas de las personas que dirigieron la década siguiente habían pasado por las mismas salas. Tennessee revocó su licencia y se incautó de la propiedad en 1961; reabrió cerca de Knoxville y continúa hoy en New Market.

items.stem: In Fayette County, Tennessee between 1959 and 1962, African Americans who registered to vote were evicted from the land they farmed and refused credit by local merchants, and hundreds lived in a settlement of tents that became known as Tent City. What does that episode show about the obstacles to Black voting in the period?
items.stemEs: En el condado de Fayette, Tennessee, entre 1959 y 1962, los afroamericanos que se inscribieron para votar fueron desalojados de las tierras que cultivaban y los comerciantes locales les negaron crédito, y cientos vivieron en un asentamiento de tiendas de campaña conocido como Tent City. ¿Qué muestra ese episodio sobre los obstáculos al voto de los negros en ese periodo?

choices.text: Economic reprisal could suppress voting where the law on paper did not, because a landlord and a merchant need no statute to act
choices.textEs: La represalia económica podía suprimir el voto donde la ley escrita no lo hacía, porque un arrendador y un comerciante no necesitan ninguna ley para actuar

choices.text: A poll tax was the chief barrier, and it was the Twenty-fourth Amendment of 1964 that finally removed it in states like Tennessee
choices.textEs: El impuesto electoral era la principal barrera, y fue la Vigésima Cuarta Enmienda de 1964 la que finalmente lo eliminó en estados como Tennessee
choices.explanation: The poll tax was real and the amendment is real. Tennessee had already abolished its own poll tax by state constitutional amendment in 1951, eight years before Tent City — so it cannot be the barrier these families met.
choices.misconception: offers the period's best-known legal barrier in a state that had already repealed it

choices.text: Federal law offered no remedy of any kind until the Voting Rights Act of 1965 put registration under federal supervision
choices.textEs: La ley federal no ofrecía remedio alguno hasta que la Ley de Derecho al Voto de 1965 puso la inscripción bajo supervisión federal
choices.explanation: The 1965 act is what finally worked at scale, so the emphasis is understandable. A remedy existed and was used here: the Civil Rights Act of 1957 created a Civil Rights Division that could sue, and it sued in Fayette County in 1960.
choices.misconception: treats the strongest later statute as the first one available

choices.text: County registrars refused to accept applications from Black residents, which was the whole of the problem in Fayette County
choices.textEs: Los registradores del condado se negaban a aceptar solicitudes de residentes negros, y ese era todo el problema en el condado de Fayette
choices.explanation: Registrars across the South did obstruct applicants and some did so here. It cannot be the whole of it in this county, because the people in the tents were those who had got past the registrar; the eviction is what happened next.
choices.misconception: stops at the barrier at the courthouse door when the episode is about what followed getting through it

items.dokRationale: The student must infer the kind of obstacle from the form the reprisal took, and distinguish it from three legal barriers that are real and are not what happened here. Naming Tent City or its dates is the DOK 1 version of this content.
items.explanation: These families had already succeeded in registering, which is what makes the episode legible: the pressure came after the courthouse, from landlords and shopkeepers who needed no statute to act and left no statute to strike down. The Justice Department sued in Fayette County in 1960 under the Civil Rights Act of 1957 and a consent decree in 1962 barred the reprisals, which is a slower remedy than a court order against a registrar.
items.explanationEs: Esas familias ya habían logrado inscribirse, y eso es lo que hace legible el episodio: la presión llegó después del tribunal, de arrendadores y comerciantes que no necesitaban ninguna ley para actuar y no dejaron ninguna ley que anular. El Departamento de Justicia demandó en el condado de Fayette en 1960 al amparo de la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1957 y un acuerdo judicial de 1962 prohibió las represalias, un remedio más lento que una orden judicial contra un registrador.

items.stem: The Nashville sit-ins of February to May 1960 desegregated downtown lunch counters faster than comparable campaigns elsewhere, and are often called the best-organised of the early sit-ins. Which feature of the campaign do most accounts credit for its discipline?
items.stemEs: Las sentadas de Nashville, de febrero a mayo de 1960, acabaron con la segregación en los mostradores de almuerzo del centro más rápido que campañas comparables en otros lugares, y a menudo se las llama las mejor organizadas de las primeras sentadas. ¿Qué señalan la mayoría de los relatos atribuyen esa disciplina?

choices.text: The sit-in movement began at Greensboro, North Carolina on the first of February 1960, and students in Nashville took it up less than two weeks afterward
choices.textEs: El movimiento de sentadas comenzó en Greensboro, Carolina del Norte, el primero de febrero de 1960, y los estudiantes de Nashville lo retomaron menos de dos semanas después
choices.explanation: The dates are right — Greensboro on the first of February, Nashville's first full sit-in on the thirteenth. It describes the sequence and not the preparation: Nashville's training workshops had been running since the previous autumn, which is the point the question asks about.
choices.misconception: answers with the order in which cities acted rather than what one of them had done beforehand

choices.text: Nashville's mayor ordered the lunch counters opened, which is why the campaign there took less time than comparable ones in other Southern cities
choices.textEs: El alcalde de Nashville ordenó abrir los mostradores de almuerzo, y por eso la campaña allí tardó menos que otras comparables en otras ciudades del sur
choices.explanation: Mayor Ben West did something close and it mattered: asked directly by Diane Nash on the steps of City Hall in April 1960 whether segregated counters were wrong, he said yes, in front of several thousand people and the press. He gave no order; the merchants opened the counters in May.
choices.misconception: turns a mayor's public admission into an order he had no power to give

choices.text: The students had trained in nonviolent discipline in workshops for months before the first sit-in, so they knew how to respond when they were attacked
choices.textEs: Los estudiantes se habían formado en la disciplina no violenta en talleres durante meses antes de la primera sentada, de modo que sabían cómo responder cuando los agredían

choices.text: Nashville's lunch counters had already been desegregated before any sit-in took place there, so the campaign met very little organised resistance
choices.textEs: Los mostradores de almuerzo de Nashville ya estaban desegregados antes de que se produjera ninguna sentada allí, de modo que la campaña encontró muy poca resistencia organizada
choices.explanation: The order is reversed and so is the resistance. The counters were segregated, roughly a hundred and fifty students were arrested, and in April the home of the movement's attorney, Z. Alexander Looby, was bombed.
choices.misconception: inverts the sequence and erases the resistance the campaign actually met

items.dokRationale: The student must identify which of four true statements about the campaign accounts for its discipline, rather than merely describing its outcome. Recalling that Nashville desegregated its counters in 1960 is the DOK 1 version.
items.explanation: The workshops came first. James Lawson had been training students in nonviolent discipline since the autumn of 1959 — before the Greensboro sit-in that is usually treated as the movement's start — so when the counters were occupied the students already knew how to be arrested, how to replace one another on the stools, and how to answer being attacked without striking back.
items.explanationEs: Los talleres fueron primero. James Lawson llevaba formando a estudiantes en la disciplina no violenta desde el otoño de 1959 — antes de la sentada de Greensboro, que suele tratarse como el comienzo del movimiento — así que cuando se ocuparon los mostradores los estudiantes ya sabían cómo ser detenidos, cómo relevarse en los taburetes y cómo responder a una agresión sin devolverla.
